sources.citation: Kuch, Larry (1993). The phonology of Birifor. [Legon]: Inst.of African Studies, Univ. of Ghana. 36 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online; also in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number 2235.17.50 no. 21)
sources.note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for malb1235, so there is nothing to agree with or contradict. Beyond that, the work describes Southern Birifor (biv, sout2790): the data are from Pastor Daniel Tampuri of Belema, Ghana, and Ratcliffe's Ghanaian wordlists; the archive.org record is tagged 'Birifor, Southern; biv'. Northern/Malba Birifor of Burkina Faso is named on p.1 only as the subject of unpublished manuscripts by Brian Woodford and Lynn Franklin. Even for Southern Birifor the work is silent on stress.

sources.citation: Tirogo, Issoufou François & Noéllie Soubeiga. 2023. Vowel length in Kasim, Samoma and Birifor. Akofena, Varia n°10, vol. 3: 437-446 (CC BY 4.0). Birifor data are the Malba parler, taken from Tirogo 2018.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on word stress/accent. §2.3 and §3.3 on Birifor: vowel length is 'a trait of the syllable' (citing Tirogo 2018: 89), CV/CVV and CVC/CVVC oppositions, then reanalysed (following Tirogo 'to appear') as two syllables (-V# a number suffix); all Birifor forms are tone-marked (và/và:, lár/lá:r, pɩ̀r/pɩ̀:r, bɛ́̃/bɛ́̃:, bɩ̀r/bɩ̀r-ɛ̀, láá/láύ, ɟúú/púó) but the words 'stress' and 'accent' never occur; the only prosodic remarks are that length is 'a prosodic fact' at the syllable level and that long vowels can bear 'modulated' (contour) tone.
